sections.html:
Hampton is an independent city on the Virginia Peninsula, which means no county government stands above it. The total area of 136.27 square miles includes only 51.46 of dry land, and water covers 62.2 percent. Elevation averages about 10 feet.

Creeks, rivers and Chesapeake Bay frontage influence nearly every sale. A waterfront street and an inland block may be minutes apart yet get treated as different products by buyers, appraisers and insurers.

On July 1, 1952 the old city, Phoebus and Elizabeth City County combined to make today's Hampton. The first settlement dates to 1610, the town was incorporated in 1705 and the city charter came in 1849. Population was 137,148 in the 2020 census, with an estimate of 137,315 for 2025.

Hampton grew out of several older communities, not one downtown with suburbs around it. Phoebus, Fox Hill, Buckroe Beach, Aberdeen Gardens, Farmington, Northampton, Newmarket and Hampton Woods are all on the list, along with Wythe and its Olde Wythe Historic District and the Victoria Boulevard Historic District.

Some houses in the historic districts are many decades old, and a few are over a century. Worn framing, original wiring and old plumbing lead many owners to sell as-is instead of paying contractors. Fort Monroe, at Old Point Comfort, was decommissioned by the Army on September 15, 2011 and became a National Monument on November 1 of that year.

Langley Air Force Base is home to the 633rd Air Base Wing and the 1st and 192nd Fighter Wings, and NASA's Langley Research Center is in town as well. Hampton University and Virginia Peninsula Community College add jobs in education.

Orders, not the housing calendar, drive these households. If a transfer takes you out of Hampton Roads, you may have only weeks to close, and a buyer's mortgage approval, appraisal and inspection could carry the sale beyond your report date. The city borders Newport News and Poquoson, with Williamsburg and Yorktown close, so many residents work in another city and judge a house by its commute.

Two bridge-tunnels define travel. I-64 crosses through the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel near downtown Hampton, and I-664 uses the Monitor-Merrimac Memorial Bridge-Tunnel a few miles off. The interstates come together near the Hampton Coliseum. U.S. 17, U.S. 60, U.S. 258 and State Routes 134 and 143 fill out the network, and buses leave from the Hampton Transit Center near downtown.

A house near a ramp or tunnel approach gains a short commute and loses some quiet. Buyers usually raise both.

Hampton has hot, humid summers and mild winters. The mean annual temperature is 60.2 degrees Fahrenheit. A typical year brings about 47 inches of rain and about 6 inches of snow, with August the wettest month.

Water is the practical concern. Between heavy rainfall and so much nearby shoreline, inspectors start with the crawl space, basement, roof and drainage. The city and federal agencies set flood zone maps and insurance rules, so look up your parcel before you pick a price.

Every year the Assessor of Real Estate values each property at 100 percent of market value. The rate on the city's page is $1.14 per $100 of assessed value, applied over a tax year from July 1 to June 30; look at the real estate tax page for the current figure when you plan your budget.

Billing stepTiming
First-half bill mailedAround November 1
First half dueDecember 5
Second-half bill mailedAround May 1
Second half dueJune 5
Late penalty10 percent after the due date
Interest on unpaid balances10 percent a year, starting July 1

Anyone who thinks an assessment is too high has three routes, laid out on the city's appeal page:

  • Office Review: apply within 30 days of the assessment notice.
  • Board of Review: apply within 60 days of the notice, with no office review required first.
  • Circuit Court: you may petition directly and skip both earlier steps.

Reach the assessor at One Franklin Street, Suite 602, or 757-727-8311, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The same handful of situations keeps turning up, and each suggests a different way to sell.

  • Heirs who inherit a house in Phoebus, Fox Hill or Wythe and cannot keep it up.
  • A military transfer with a firm report date.
  • A frame house with deferred work on the roof, drainage or moisture.
  • A rental with tenants still living in it.
  • Property tax or a mortgage that has fallen behind.

A house in good shape, with time on your side, may sell for more on the open market. The price of that route is showings, inspection requests and a buyer who might still be arranging a loan. Cash gives up part of the price and gets you speed and a closing that holds. Before taking any offer, get it in writing, learn who pays title costs, and subtract repairs, commission and months of carrying costs from the listing price to see your real net.

sections.h2: Selling for cash, one step at a time
sections.html:
Without a lender, the calendar is controlled by the title work. We begin by talking through the house, view photos or visit, and send a written offer. After you agree, a title or settlement company runs the closing.

Before that day, the company's search turns up liens, unpaid taxes and other filings against the owner, including any installment tied to December 5 or June 5. Should the owner have died, the company will ask who is authorized to sell, so locate those papers early. You decide the closing date inside what the search permits, and you are bound by nothing until you sign.

Bring the deed, the latest tax bill, any loan payoff figure and, for a rental, the lease. A tenant who stays after the sale keeps the rights the lease gives. Ask the title officer to explain any line on the settlement statement that looks unfamiliar, and keep a copy of every document you sign.

A little preparation makes any Hampton sale smoother, whoever the buyer turns out to be. Pull out the deed and the newest tax bill, and write down whatever is still owed on the property, including a loan balance. If a roof leak, damp crawl space or flooding history is part of the story, say so up front, since an honest description keeps the price from shifting later.

  • Know whether you are in a historic district, and ask the city about any exterior rules.
  • Look up your flood zone so you can answer a buyer's first insurance question.
  • List repairs you know about, even if you do not plan to fix them.
  • Decide how soon you need to close, and why that date matters.

faqs.a: The city spans 136.27 square miles, but only 51.46 are land. Population was 137,148 in 2020 and is estimated at 137,315 for 2025.

faqs.q: Does Hampton have a county government?
faqs.a: No county sits above Hampton. It is an independent city that absorbed Elizabeth City County and Phoebus on July 1, 1952, and it handles assessments and billing itself.

faqs.q: What are the Hampton tax due dates?
faqs.a: Half the year's bill is due December 5 and the other half June 5. Pay late and a 10 percent penalty applies.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Hampton assessment?
faqs.a: The office review window is 30 days from your notice, and the Board of Review accepts applications for 60 days. You may also petition Circuit Court without trying either of those first.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Hampton house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Plenty of local houses are older and need work, and in an as-is cash sale you fix nothing before closing. The offer simply reflects the house's condition.
